subject: principles-of-flight
source_policy: Use the approved POF handbook as technical source of truth. Question-bank and mock-exam material may confirm exam wording/mapping but must not override handbook physics.

concepts.concept: Lift is produced by a pressure difference: lower pressure above the aerofoil and higher pressure below it create a net upward force
concepts.reuse_justification: Both questions ask for the same pressure distribution around a lifting aerofoil: high pressure below and low pressure above.

source.notes: Bernoulli section and Figures 1-9/1-10 show accelerating flow over the upper surface, lower pressure above, higher pressure below, and the resulting lift force.

brief.student_must_understand: A lifting aerofoil has lower static pressure above and higher static pressure below, so the pressure imbalance produces a net upward lift force.
refine: Make high/low pressure zones immediately readable
Use sparse pressure arrows without clutter
Keep airflow and lift vectors physically consistent

concepts.mapping_reason: The two questions directly ask which pressure distribution creates lift; the visual will show that exact upper/lower pressure relationship.

concepts.concept: Adverse aileron yaw becomes more noticeable at high angle of attack because the down-going aileron adds angle of attack and induced drag to a wing already operating at higher AoA
concepts.reuse_justification: All four questions test the same relationship: adverse aileron yaw increases as baseline angle of attack increases.

source.notes: Figure 1-30 shows the lowered aileron increasing local AoA and lift. The handbook induced-drag section on page 8 states induced drag increases directly with angle of attack; together they explain why adverse yaw is stronger at high AoA.

brief.student_must_understand: For the same roll input, a higher baseline AoA creates a larger induced-drag difference between the wings, so adverse yaw is stronger.
refine: Compare LOW AoA versus HIGH AoA side by side
Show larger drag imbalance only in the high-AoA case
Keep local AoA and yaw arrows unambiguous
add: Adverse yaw stronger at HIGH AoA takeaway

concepts.mapping_reason: The questions ask when adverse yaw is most noticeable or how it changes with AoA; a low-vs-high AoA comparison teaches that exact relationship.

concepts.concept: In subsonic flow through a narrowing venturi, mass flow remains constant while velocity increases and static pressure decreases in the throat

source.notes: The handbook venturi explanation states that as the passage narrows it contains the same amount of fluid, while flow speed rises and pressure falls.

brief.student_must_understand: A smaller venturi area does not lose mass flow: the flow speeds up through the throat and static pressure falls.
refine: Make area, velocity and pressure changes readable at a glance
Keep inlet and throat states visually paired

concepts.mapping_reason: Question 1966 tests the exact continuity/Bernoulli changes through a venturi throat, which the visual will label directly.

concepts.concept: In a level banked turn, the tilted lift vector has a vertical component that supports weight and a horizontal component that provides centripetal force; more lift/AoA is required and the resultant wing load rises
concepts.reuse_justification: All eight questions test one banked-turn force system: centripetal force comes from the horizontal component of wing lift, vertical lift must still support weight, and the higher resultant load is produced by the turn.

source.notes: The handbook explains that banking makes wing lift pull the aeroplane into a curved path, that constant altitude requires increased wing lift/load, and Figures 1-33/1-34 show load rising with bank. Page 25 explains the weight-plus-turning-load resultant.

brief.student_must_understand: Bank tilts lift: its vertical component must equal weight to hold altitude, while its horizontal component turns the aeroplane inward; achieving the larger total lift requires increased AoA and creates a higher load factor.
preserve: Total lift perpendicular to wing plane
refine: Resolve lift into vertical and horizontal components
Point the horizontal component toward the centre of turn
Show the increased resultant/load without mixing centripetal and centrifugal reference frames

concepts.mapping_reason: These questions all ask about the same level-turn force balance, its centripetal source, the AoA increase needed to maintain altitude, or the associated resultant load.

concepts.concept: For a conventional propeller turning clockwise as seen from the cockpit, torque reaction tends to roll left and asymmetric blade effect/P-factor produces a left-yaw tendency that is corrected with right rudder
concepts.reuse_justification: Both questions test linked propeller-induced left-turning tendencies under the same conventional clockwise-propeller condition: torque reaction for roll and P-factor/asymmetric blade loading for yaw/rudder correction.

source.notes: The handbook identifies torque reaction and asymmetric propeller loading/P-factor as left-turning forces, notes the tendency is strongest at high power/low speed/high AoA, and states right rudder is used to correct it. The torque-reaction detail continues on page 14.

brief.student_must_understand: Clockwise propeller from the cockpit: torque reaction rolls the aircraft left; at high power/high AoA the descending blade produces more thrust, yawing left, so right rudder is required.
refine: Use a two-panel torque versus P-factor layout
Do not conflate roll from torque with yaw from P-factor
add: High power + low speed + high AoA emphasis

concepts.mapping_reason: Question 1948 asks the torque-reaction roll direction and question 1950 asks the P-factor/right-rudder correction; the two-panel visual separates those exact effects.
